opus-5.5.text:
I think it's worth separating two questions: why the humanoid form at all, and how far the resemblance should go.

On the first, the strongest argument for humanoids isn't aesthetic. It's that the world is already built for the human body. Doorknobs, stairs, kitchen counters, tools, car seats: everything assumes roughly our height, two arms, two hands with opposable thumbs, and a way of walking. If you want a general-purpose robot that can step into an existing factory or home without rebuilding the environment, the human shape is a very good prior.

There's also a data argument, which matters a lot to me as someone working on world models and physical AI. We have an enormous amount of video of humans doing things: cooking, assembling, cleaning, playing sports. If the robot's body is close to ours, it becomes much easier to transfer knowledge from that data. A model that understands how a human hand grasps a cup can more readily map that onto a robot hand with similar kinematics. The further the embodiment drifts from ours, the larger that translation gap becomes.

But that doesn't mean the robot needs to look like a person in the cosmetic sense. I don't think realistic skin or a lifelike face adds much functional value, and it can push you into the uncanny valley, where people feel uneasy instead of comfortable. What matters is functional resemblance: proportions, degrees of freedom, reach, dexterity, and the ability to balance and move through spaces designed for people.

And where it makes sense, I think we should be pragmatic and even go beyond the human design. A robot's wrist could rotate continuously. It could have extra sensors, like cameras in its palms. It doesn't need to tire, and its joints don't have to share our limits. Humanoid is a starting point that unlocks compatibility with our world and our data, not a constraint we have to copy faithfully.

So my short answer: close enough in form and function to use human environments and learn from human experience, but not so close that we copy our limitations or chase realism for its own sake. Ultimately the intelligence, the robot's ability to understand and predict the physical world, will matter much more than how human it looks.

r001.rationale: The response says human environments are built around human proportions and abilities, making humanoid form a strong fit for general-purpose robots operating in existing homes and factories.

r002.rationale: The response discusses functional compatibility, data transfer, and avoiding unnecessary realism, but does not identify economic efficiency as the ultimate deciding factor.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I get asked a lot, and my honest answer is that I don't think the goal should be to make robots look as human as possible. The goal should be to make them useful in a world that was built for humans.

Think about where these robots need to operate. Our factories, our warehouses, our homes, our hospitals. Every doorway, every staircase, every shelf, every tool was designed around the human body. If you want a general-purpose robot that can go into those environments without rebuilding everything, the human form factor is a very practical starting point. Two legs, two arms, roughly our height, hands that can grasp the same objects we grasp. That's the part of "humanoid" that really matters to me. It's about compatibility with the physical world, not about looks.

There's also a data argument that I care about a lot. We have enormous amounts of video of humans doing things. If the robot's body is close to a human body, then human demonstrations become much more directly useful for training. The mapping from what a person does to what the robot should do becomes simpler. So the morphology isn't just an engineering convenience, it's also a way to unlock the data we already have.

But beyond that functional similarity, I think chasing a perfectly human appearance is mostly a distraction, and sometimes counterproductive. People are very sensitive to faces and skin. If you get ninety-five percent of the way there, it can feel more unsettling than something that is clearly a machine. And from a practical point of view, a lot of what makes a human look human, the fine facial expressions, the realistic skin, doesn't help the robot pick up a box or fold laundry. It adds cost and complexity without adding capability.

So the way I'd put it is: humanoid in function, honest in form. Let the robot be shaped by the tasks and the environment. If that means it has a screen instead of a face, or an extra joint in the wrist that no human has, that's fine. We're not trying to recreate a person. We're trying to build a partner that fits into our world and can learn from how we live in it.

The one place where appearance does matter is trust. If a robot is going to work next to people, especially in homes or with elderly folks, it needs to be predictable and non-threatening. But I think that comes more from behavior, from moving smoothly and communicating intent clearly, than from how closely it mimics a human face.

r001.rationale: The response says human-designed factories, homes, and other spaces make a human-like body a practical starting point for general-purpose robots.

r002.rationale: It mentions added cost and complexity, but does not identify economic efficiency as the ultimate factor deciding how closely robots should resemble humans.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on what we want the robot to do. There’s a practical reason to give a robot a human-like body: our environments are designed for humans. Stairs, doors, tools—the robot needs to interact with all of those. But that doesn’t necessarily mean it needs a face that looks exactly like a person.

I would separate resemblance from capability. Can it move safely around us? Can it manipulate objects? Can we understand what it’s about to do? Those are more useful goals than making it visually indistinguishable from a human. For some applications, a more human-like appearance might help people interact with it. For others, a clearly mechanical appearance could work just as well. I’d let the application drive that choice.

r001.rationale: The response says human-designed environments such as stairs, doors, and tools give robots a practical reason to have human-like bodies so they can interact with them.

r002.rationale: The response says the application should drive the choice, but does not identify economic efficiency as the ultimate deciding factor.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it depends on what we want the robot to do. Our homes and workplaces are designed around the human body, so having two arms, hands, and legs can be useful. It allows a robot to operate in those environments without requiring us to redesign everything.

But that doesn’t mean the robot needs to look exactly like a person. I would separate the functional aspect from the appearance. Hands need to be capable of manipulating objects; a face doesn’t necessarily need to look human. For me, the priority is whether the robot can perform useful tasks safely and reliably. Its resemblance to a human should serve that purpose.

r001.rationale: The response says human-designed homes and workplaces make arms, hands, and legs useful, but it does not identify fully humanoid robots as best suited to diverse operations.

r002.rationale: The response prioritizes useful tasks, safety, and reliability; it does not identify economic efficiency as the ultimate deciding factor.
